$comment: The self-probe gate's cost ceiling, in seconds, checked in CI against the evidence the probe already writes. Raising this is a reviewable diff with a reason, which is the entire point: the gate went from 9.6 to 23.6 minutes across one merged pull request and nothing said a word. Growth is allowed; going unnoticed is not. Budget the TOTAL and never a per-fault average — the regression that prompted this raised the fault count from 59 to 91 while per-fault cost barely moved, so an average would have reported everything fine.

measured.how: probe . --include-dirty --budget 180000 --cost, from scratch, idle developer machine, after the shared-defender cut
measured.note: LOCAL. Not comparable with measuredInCI and not what this budget is set from. The previous local from-scratch figure (1168 s, 129 faults) was taken on a contended machine, so 1168 -> 816 overstates the cut.

headroom: The v0.10.1 release job measured 1210 s from scratch at 154 faults. TG-HOMEBREW-TAP-IS-PUBLISHED deliberately adds four integration-defended faults measured at 53 s on the Node 22 PR leg, for an expected cold total near 1263 s. 1440 is ~14% above that figure: enough for normal CI variance, while a 59-to-91 style jump (+76%) still fails. Budget against the from-scratch release job, never a pull-request run that may reuse verdicts. The four sweep self-claims added in the sweep PR (6 faults) measure 11.1 s locally across 36 runs, worst claim 3.9 s — inside the 100 s per-claim ceiling and inside the headroom above, so the budget is NOT raised for them. They fault pure functions in spec/lib/validate.mjs, src/sweep/sweep.mjs and src/supply/select.mjs and are defended by unit tests, which is the shape nextCut.done recommends. The sweep acceptance test (test/sweep.fixture.test.mjs, ~1.8 s) is not named as any claim defender, so it costs the suite and not the probe.

history.why: First budget. Set from the 804 s measurement after #73 cut the gate from 1414 s.

#82 added eight unit-defended faults (~30 s in CI) and main went 906 -> 981 s from scratch, red against 950. Re-pointing the two replay-defended calibration claims onto pure tests took it to 962 s. The remaining overage was the budget itself: set 18% over a local 804 s, it was 4.6% over the 906 s CI already measured. Raised to 1100 against the CI figure. The heavy claims it names — TG-ADMIT-NEEDS-ALL-KILLED 87 s, TG-PROBE-NEVER-EDITS-THE-TREE-IT-MEASURES 70 s, the two TG-MCP-* at 42 s — are the next #73-style cut, tracked separately.

The 0.8.1 field-report fixes added 6 claims and 14 faults (115 -> 129 faults, 690 -> 774 runs, +12.2%) and ci.yml measured 1123 s against 1100, over by 23 s. Two things make 1123 the wrong number to budget against, in opposite directions. It is LOW: the run restored a cache under the `self-evidence-` fallback key, so claims whose target and defenders were untouched reused their verdict, and this budget is defined against a from-scratch probe because the release job is from scratch. It is also not the whole story: 46 s of the growth was avoidable and already removed — the new calibration claim's tests are pure but were added to replay.test.mjs, whose scripted-corpus setup costs tens of seconds a run, and re-pointing them at calibration.test.mjs took that claim from 51 s to 4.9 s. A from-scratch local run of the same commit measured 1168 s on a contended machine. 1350 is ~14% over an expected from-scratch CI figure of ~1185, which is the same headroom rule that set 1100 against 962. Expected to come DOWN: the shared-defender cut below is the next piece of work and should return the gate to under 900 s.

Tightened from 1350 once a FROM-SCRATCH figure existed. 1350 was set defensively against a reuse-affected 1123 s, because this budget is defined against a from-scratch probe and none had run yet. release.yml then measured 1081 s at 129 faults / 774 runs on the v0.9.0 release commit with no reuse: 129 faults cost 1081 s against 115 faults at 999 s, so +82 s for +14 faults. 1230 is ~14% over 1081, the same headroom rule that set 1100 against 962. Leaving 1350 in place would have let a 25% regression pass unnoticed, which is the opposite of what this file is for.

The v0.10.1 release job supplied the next from-scratch measurement: 1210 s at 154 faults / 924 runs on 70e9d61. The old 1230 s ceiling therefore had only 1.7% headroom before this PR. The live-Homebrew-tap field fix adds one integration-defended claim, four faults and 24 runs; the Node 22 PR leg measured that claim at 53 s and the total at 1243 s with verdict reuse. Adding the deliberate 53 s to the cold release baseline projects ~1263 s. 1440 restores the established ~14% CI headroom without changing the 100 s per-claim ceiling.

measuredInCI.how: release.yml test: probe . --budget 180000 --cost, from scratch on the v0.10.1 release commit. No verdict reuse, which is what this budget is defined against.

before.note: the v0.9.0 release job, before the v0.10 adoption claims

reuseAffected.note: ci.yml figures are NOT comparable with this one. Its cache restore-key chain ends in a bare 'self-evidence-' prefix, so any previous evidence can be restored regardless of claims hash, and a reused record contributes what it cost when it was last probed on another runner. The same commit reported 1123 s and then 1025 s. Correctness is unaffected - TG-REUSE-NEVER-CROSSES-A-FAULT-EDIT re-probes any changed fault - only the reported total moves.

done.why: faults classify(), a pure function; was defended by negative-control.test.mjs, which spawns real runners against fixture repositories
faults labelDiff(), pure; was defended by replay.test.mjs, which builds a scripted git corpus

nextCut.expectedInCI: The projected ~145 s cut was real, but later behavior coverage spent the savings: v0.10.1 measured 1210 s from scratch at 154 faults. Future cuts must be confirmed against a release job and must not trade end-to-end coverage for seconds.
nextCut.remaining: The eight claims still on negative-control.test.mjs and replay.test.mjs fault probe.mjs, the runners and git-walking code, where the expensive fixture is the point. Forcing those onto unit tests would trade real end-to-end coverage for seconds.
nextCut.rule: A claim whose fault lands in a pure module should have a pure defender. All three cuts above fit that shape, and so did the 51 s calibration claim before them. This is mechanically checkable — compare the imports of the faulted file against those of its defenders — and is the shape of a future `claims --lint`.

perClaim.why: A SECOND ceiling, because neither unit works alone. The total can only ever be raised - claims should grow forever - so a number that always goes up stops being read. A per-fault average is worse: the regression that prompted this budget raised the fault count 59 to 91 while per-fault cost barely moved, so an average would have reported everything fine. The measured pathology is per-CLAIM, and specifically a claim naming an expensive SHARED defender file, because a claim pays for every test in the file it names. TG-ADMIT-NEEDS-ALL-KILLED costs 67 s for ONE fault; a new calibration claim landed at 51 s for two purely by being written into replay.test.mjs rather than calibration.test.mjs, and re-pointing it took it to 4.9 s. The total absorbed that silently; this does not.
perClaim.rule: No new claim may be worse than the worst we already have. 75 s sits just above today's worst, so the ceiling stays meaningful as claims are added and should be tightened as the shared-defender cut lands.

todayWorst.where: CI (ci.yml test 22); the same claim measures 66.5 s locally

perClaim.calibratedAgainst: CI, never local. 75 s was set from a local 66.5 s and tripped on the very first CI run, where the same claim costs 87 s — a CI runner is materially slower, and this file already says so for the total: 950 s was 18% over local 804 s but only 4.6% over CI's 906 s, and the first PR adding any claim tripped it. The same error, one level down. 100 s is ~15% over the CI worst.
